cirrhosis patients show a task-dependent psychometric slowing with a clear trend of a higher number of incongruent errors in the Stroop Task.

cirrhotics present a task-dependent psychometric slowing and increased errors in the Stroop incongruent condition, with the patients with an altered electroencephalogram performing the Stroop significantly more slowly than those without electroencephalographic alterations and with a higher trend to a higher number of Stroop errors in the incongurent condition.

1) Cirrhotics present a psychomotor slowing and a reduced selective attention control, 2) Class C patients have a selective slowing and a reduced ability to perform the incongruent Stroop condition, 3) Patients with an altered EEG have a selective slowing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the attentional functioning of cirrhotic patients.
the study of attention in cirrhotic patients, a population that has been little investigated in the past.
the study of the attention system in cirrhotic patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cirrhotics present a selective slowing of attention, with no impairment of automatic orienting and focusing of attention.
the AAS is the first attention system to be altered in cirrhotic patients, while the PAS is preserved.

the attention system in cirrhotic patients, even in the early stages of the disease, is not fully functional and is more sensitive to alterations than in healthy subjects, but that the PAS is more resistant to alterations than the AAS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
attention is not a single function but rather a complex network of processes.
the AAS is the most sensitive attention system in cirrhotic patients, whereas the PAS is the least sensitive.
attention deficits are more evident in patients with advanced liver disease and/or hepatic encephapathy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

attention dysfunction in cirrhotic patients is not a global alteration, but a selective dysfunction in the AAS, with a selective slowing of the Strooop task and an increased percentage error in the incongruence condition of the Stoop test.
the AAS is impaired in cirrhotic patients and that this impairment is associated with the severity of hepatic encepalopathy and with the presence of an altered EEG.
cirrhotic patients have an attention deficit, especially in the early stages of the disease.
